articles.body:
Five squares of fabric—each four inches on a side, some dyed and some undyed—are the center of a National Institute of Standards and Technology experiment in making textile sorting more measurable.

The set is Research Grade Test Material 10279, Textiles for Feedstock Identification. NIST developed it as a common object that laboratories, recyclers and manufacturers can scan with their own equipment, then use to compare how reliably different systems identify fibers.

That comparison matters because textile sorting is increasingly a machine-learning and measurement problem. Clothing can be labeled incorrectly, contain blended fibers or arrive too worn for a tag to settle the question. If one facility's scanner calls a swatch cotton and another reads the same material differently, automated sorting cannot produce a predictable feedstock.

A common method is near-infrared spectroscopy. A handheld or conveyor-mounted sensor shines near-infrared light on fabric and records how the material absorbs or scatters it. The resulting spectrum acts like a molecular fingerprint. Classification software then compares that signal with known examples to infer fiber content.

NIST says facilities also use computer vision, which sorts by color and visible appearance, and hyperspectral systems that combine imaging with spectral measurements. The new material is meant to test the measurement layer beneath those tools, not to declare one sorting architecture the winner.

RGTM 10279 contains five fabric types. NIST has deliberately withheld their fiber composition while participating laboratories analyze the squares. That blind structure is the point: researchers can compare reported results without telling participants the answer in advance.

Research Grade Test Materials are faster, more exploratory cousins of NIST's fully characterized standard reference materials. Laboratories receive them in exchange for measurements and feedback that help the agency decide whether the candidate is fit for purpose and what a better-characterized successor should contain.

The agency's study runs through Sept. 30. Its initial free-order window closed July 30. NIST says the results supplied by participating organizations will remain anonymous and will feed into development of a more thoroughly analyzed reference material.

The project also connects physical standards to open data. In March, NIST released NIR-SORT 2.0, an expanded public dataset of near-infrared spectra for textiles. A shared dataset helps researchers train and test classifiers; a shared physical sample lets them check whether instruments and methods agree on the same material in the real world.

NIST researchers say the benchmark could eventually help with production quality control, detecting fiber blends not reported on labels and assessing AI-assisted sorting. They also noted a possible use in fashion authentication, while explicitly saying that authentication is not part of their current work.

The immediate claim is narrower than the supply-chain promise. RGTM 10279 is a candidate under evaluation, not a certified fix for textile waste. The study has not yet published performance results, and NIST has not quantified how much the material might improve sorting accuracy, recycling volume or costs.

bodyBlocks.text: Five squares of fabric—each four inches on a side, some dyed and some undyed—are the center of a National Institute of Standards and Technology experiment in making textile sorting more measurable.

The set is Research Grade Test Material 10279, Textiles for Feedstock Identification. NIST developed it as a common object that laboratories, recyclers and manufacturers can scan with their own equipment, then use to compare how reliably different systems identify fibers.

That comparison matters because textile sorting is increasingly a machine-learning and measurement problem. Clothing can be labeled incorrectly, contain blended fibers or arrive too worn for a tag to settle the question. If one facility's scanner calls a swatch cotton and another reads the same material differently, automated sorting cannot produce a predictable feedstock.
A physical benchmark for machine sorting

A common method is near-infrared spectroscopy. A handheld or conveyor-mounted sensor shines near-infrared light on fabric and records how the material absorbs or scatters it. The resulting spectrum acts like a molecular fingerprint. Classification software then compares that signal with known examples to infer fiber content.

bodyBlocks.alt: Diagram comparing handheld and conveyor-belt near-infrared textile sorting, with sample cotton and polyester spectra.
bodyBlocks.caption: NIST's workflow shows handheld and conveyor-belt near-infrared textile classification.
bodyBlocks.credit: NIST

bodyBlocks.text: NIST says facilities also use computer vision, which sorts by color and visible appearance, and hyperspectral systems that combine imaging with spectral measurements. The new material is meant to test the measurement layer beneath those tools, not to declare one sorting architecture the winner.

RGTM 10279 contains five fabric types. NIST has deliberately withheld their fiber composition while participating laboratories analyze the squares. That blind structure is the point: researchers can compare reported results without telling participants the answer in advance.

bodyBlocks.alt: A hand holds a sealed package containing a dark fabric square labeled Research Grade Test Material 10279 Fabric A.
bodyBlocks.caption: Fabric A is one of five blind samples in RGTM 10279.
bodyBlocks.credit: A. Boss/NIST

bodyBlocks.text: What the study can—and cannot—show

Research Grade Test Materials are faster, more exploratory cousins of NIST's fully characterized standard reference materials. Laboratories receive them in exchange for measurements and feedback that help the agency decide whether the candidate is fit for purpose and what a better-characterized successor should contain.

The agency's study runs through Sept. 30. Its initial free-order window closed July 30. NIST says the results supplied by participating organizations will remain anonymous and will feed into development of a more thoroughly analyzed reference material.

The project also connects physical standards to open data. In March, NIST released NIR-SORT 2.0, an expanded public dataset of near-infrared spectra for textiles. A shared dataset helps researchers train and test classifiers; a shared physical sample lets them check whether instruments and methods agree on the same material in the real world.

NIST researchers say the benchmark could eventually help with production quality control, detecting fiber blends not reported on labels and assessing AI-assisted sorting. They also noted a possible use in fashion authentication, while explicitly saying that authentication is not part of their current work.
NIST's July 9 announcement describes the five samples, blind interlaboratory study and Sept. 30 study end date.

A prototype carrier nicknamed the “coral torpedo” helped NOAA divers move lab-reared corals into the dim middle-light zone of the Gulf this spring, where the team planted 26 specimens on artificial reef structures at a depth of 66 meters, or about 217 feet.

The operation aboard NOAA Ship Nancy Foster combined laboratory propagation, specialized diving and new delivery hardware in an effort to rebuild mesophotic coral communities injured by the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill.

NOAA Fisheries reported the mission July 23. It said divers also relocated 16 coral fragments in the field to start new colonies—the first time rebreather divers had propagated these corals underwater and the first time divers had outplanted lab-reared mesophotic corals.

Corals previously traveled on large weighted “elevators” that resisted the water and were cumbersome to maneuver. The new streamlined tube, developed by NOAA fisheries biologist Chris Gardner, held prepared fragments and descended rapidly to a precise site where divers could remove and place them.

Speed matters because transported corals must move through changing water conditions without unnecessary mixing or handling. At depth, human divers could fit the small bases attached to the specimens into their intended positions on dome-shaped concrete structures.

The team completed decompression dives reaching 72.5 meters, or 237 feet. Closed-circuit rebreathers recycled breathing gas and extended bottom time, while a safety team and hyperbaric physician supported the operation.

Three soft-coral species were part of the planting work: Swiftia exserta, Muricea pendula and Thesea nivea. Mesophotic ecosystems live below shallow reefs but still receive some light, and they provide habitat that supports the Gulf food web.

NOAA said the crew collected 48 sediment cores and 51 live biological samples, sampled 11 colonies without removing them, mapped more than 14 square nautical miles of seafloor and collected water for organic-matter and environmental-DNA analysis.

The team also deployed three hydrophones to study whether habitat sound correlates with coral settlement and recorded stereo-camera surveys that can help researchers compare wild colony size with laboratory specimens.

Those measurements are the baseline for the harder question: whether the transplanted and newly propagated colonies survive and grow. NOAA has not yet reported long-term survival rates from this mission and says monitoring will continue.

The expedition is part of the Mesophotic and Deep Benthic Communities restoration portfolio led by NOAA for the Deepwater Horizon Open Ocean Trustee Implementation Group. A successful planting is a milestone, but ecological recovery will be measured over years rather than one voyage.

NOAA’s latest week-two hazards outlook places three very different risks on the same national map: extreme heat across much of the South, heavy monsoon rain in the Southwest and the possibility of rapid-onset drought in parts of the Plains and Mississippi Valley.

The Climate Prediction Center product, issued Aug. 5 for the period Aug. 13 through Aug. 19, is a regional risk assessment rather than a day-by-day local forecast. It highlights where forecast models and recent conditions support elevated concern eight to 14 days ahead.

A moderate risk of extreme heat covers parts of the Southern and Central Plains and the Lower Mississippi Valley for Aug. 12 through Aug. 15. A wider slight-risk area extends across much of the south-central United States, Southeast and Mid-Atlantic through Aug. 18.

NOAA tied the heat risk to persistent high pressure and humid air moving north from the Gulf. Its combined GEFS and ECMWF tool showed at least a 40% chance across broad areas that maximum temperature or heat index would exceed the local 90th percentile at some point during the period.

The strongest modeled signal reached as high as 70% in parts of the Lower Mississippi Valley. Those probabilities describe conditions relative to local climate, not a single temperature threshold shared by every city.

The outlook discontinued an earlier heat-risk area for the Intermountain West and Northern Plains as models increasingly favored a West Coast trough and moderating temperatures there. Forecast confidence was higher in the southern heat signal than in earlier runs, the discussion said.

The same developing western trough may help draw more moisture into the Southwest monsoon. NOAA posted a moderate risk of heavy precipitation for parts of the Desert Southwest and southern Great Basin from Aug. 12 through Aug. 14, with a broader slight-risk area lasting through Aug. 18.

Model ensembles showed widespread chances above 50% for three-day precipitation totals to exceed half an inch in parts of the region, with smaller areas carrying a 20% chance of more than one inch. In dry washes and canyons, relatively modest totals can still produce flash flooding.

A separate slight-risk area for heavy precipitation covers parts of the Great Lakes, Ohio Valley and Upper Mississippi Valley early in the period. NOAA said humid air and possible mesoscale convective systems could support intense rainfall, while acknowledging that models disagreed on the evolving upper-level pattern.

Parts of the Central and Southern Plains, the Ozarks and the Lower and Middle Mississippi Valley carry a rapid-onset drought designation. NOAA cited 30-day precipitation deficits greater than two inches in portions of that area, along with continued heat and dryness into mid-August.

Rapid-onset drought is not simply a long dry spell. It describes deterioration that accelerates over weeks as limited rain combines with high temperatures, wind and atmospheric demand for moisture. The risk designation signals favorable conditions for that process; it does not certify that every county inside the boundary will enter drought.

Because the product looks more than a week ahead, exact hazard boundaries and timing can shift. NOAA directs readers to local National Weather Service offices for short-range, location-specific forecasts and warnings.

The larger lesson is visible in the map’s contrasts. A stronger monsoon can raise flash-flood risk in the Southwest while persistent heat and rainfall deficits worsen soil moisture farther east. National weather does not move as one condition, even within the same forecast week.

The Federal Reserve’s preferred broad inflation gauge fell 0.1% in June while inflation-adjusted consumer spending increased 0.4%, according to estimates released July 30 by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.

The monthly decline in the headline personal consumption expenditures price index contrasted with a 0.1% increase in the index excluding food and energy. Compared with June 2025, the headline index was up 3.7% and the core index was up 3.3%. Monthly and year-over-year readings measure different periods and should not be treated as interchangeable.

Current-dollar personal consumption expenditures rose by $65.2 billion, or 0.3%, in June. BEA attributed $58.2 billion of that increase to services and $7.0 billion to goods. After adjusting for price changes, real consumer spending increased by $68.0 billion, also reported as a 0.4% monthly gain.

Personal income increased by $54.9 billion, or 0.2%, while disposable personal income rose by $48.3 billion, or 0.2%. Real disposable income increased 0.3%. Personal saving was $646.1 billion, and the personal saving rate was 2.7% of disposable income.

The combination of rising real spending and a lower headline price index is not contradictory. Current-dollar spending measures the amount paid, while real spending removes estimated price changes. A negative monthly headline reading also does not mean every consumer price fell; it means the weighted PCE price index declined overall from May to June.

BEA said the increase in personal income primarily reflected higher compensation, income from assets and government social benefits, partly offset by lower farm proprietors’ income. The compensation increase was led by private wages and salaries using Bureau of Labor Statistics employment data.

The agency also revised estimates for April and May after receiving updated employment, Medicaid and Treasury data. Like other monthly national-account estimates, the June figures are preliminary and can change as more complete source information becomes available.

The June report therefore shows a one-month decline in the broad PCE price index alongside continued growth in real consumer spending, but it does not establish that inflation has permanently reversed. The 12-month measures remained positive, and the next Personal Income and Outlays release is scheduled for August 26.

articles.body:
Four Senate Democrats reintroduced a proposal July 22 that would create a new Supreme Court appointment every two years and limit participation in the Court’s appellate docket to the nine most recently appointed justices.

Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, Cory Booker of New Jersey, Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Alex Padilla of California announced the Supreme Court Biennial Appointments and Term Limits Act of 2026. Seven additional Democratic senators are listed as cosponsors in the draft released by Whitehouse’s office.

The proposal is commonly described as an 18-year term-limit bill, but its legal design is more specific. It would not remove a justice from federal judicial office after 18 years.

Instead, only the nine most recently appointed justices who are available would hear cases within the Supreme Court’s appellate jurisdiction. Justices outside that group would continue to hear cases within the Court’s original jurisdiction and could perform other duties required by law.

The practical result would ordinarily give a justice 18 years on the full appellate docket if a new appointment occurs every two years.

The bill would require the president to nominate one Supreme Court justice within the first 120 days of the first and third years of a presidential term, subject to Senate confirmation.

It contains procedures for withdrawn or rejected nominations and for filling vacancies when fewer than nine justices remain.

The proposal would not take effect immediately. The draft says it would begin with the first full presidential term starting after enactment.

Supporters say regular appointments would reduce the political stakes of unpredictable vacancies and prevent a single appointment from shaping the Court for several decades.

The constitutional argument is less settled than the sponsors’ announcement suggests.

Article III says federal judges hold their offices during good behavior, a foundation for life tenure unless a judge retires, resigns, dies or is removed through impeachment. The proposal attempts to preserve that tenure by leaving every justice in office while changing which justices hear appellate cases.

The Constitution also gives Congress authority to make exceptions and regulations concerning the Supreme Court’s appellate jurisdiction. The sponsors rely on that power to argue that Congress can structure participation in appellate cases without constitutionally removing a justice.

Opponents are likely to argue that Congress cannot use its jurisdictional authority to achieve indirectly what would otherwise require a constitutional amendment, especially if the law effectively displaces a sitting justice from the Court’s central work.

That dispute has not been conclusively resolved by the Supreme Court. Similar reform proposals have been debated by scholars and lawmakers, but this specific statutory structure has not been tested through a final judgment.

The draft also raises operational questions. It would allow a justice who ordinarily hears only original-jurisdiction cases to substitute when an active-docket justice is unavailable because of disability, recusal or disqualification.

The measure does not guarantee that the Senate will confirm a nominee on schedule. It requires presidential appointments but cannot erase the Senate’s advice-and-consent power or political conflict over confirmation.

The proposal’s future is uncertain in the current Congress. The announcing senators are Democrats, and the release identifies no Republican sponsor.

Even without immediate passage, the bill defines one of the principal statutory approaches to Supreme Court term limits: preserve formal life tenure, regularize appointments and use appellate jurisdiction to rotate the nine-justice active docket.

The draft also raises operational questions. It would allow a justice who ordinarily hears only original-jurisdiction cases to substitute when an active-docket justice is unavailable because of disability, recusal or disqualification.

The measure does not guarantee that the Senate will confirm a nominee on schedule. It requires presidential appointments but cannot erase the Senate’s advice-and-consent power or political conflict over confirmation.
The proposal’s future is uncertain in the current Congress. The announcing senators are Democrats, and the release identifies no Republican sponsor.

Even without immediate passage, the bill defines one of the principal statutory approaches to Supreme Court term limits: preserve formal life tenure, regularize appointments and use appellate jurisdiction to rotate the nine-justice active docket.

A Texas producer recalled 1,589,577 dozen shell eggs—roughly 19.1 million individual eggs—after environmental monitoring found a potential for Salmonella Enteritidis contamination, according to a company announcement posted by the Food and Drug Administration.

The recall is broad enough to cross brands and package sizes, but it is not a recall of every Kroger, Simple Truth, Brookshire’s, Country Morning or Sunups carton. The controlling identifiers are printed on the side: plant code P-1950 or the numeric code printed as 840962 or 0840962, plus a Julian date from 157 through 184.

Affected cartons have sell-by or best-by dates between July 20 and Aug. 17, 2026. The notice says the eggs were produced at two Texas farms and distributed between June 6 and July 3.

Midwest Poultry Services says the eggs went to foodservice and retail customers in Texas, Oklahoma and Louisiana. The notice separately identifies Kroger stores in Texas and Louisiana and Brookshire Grocery stores in Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Louisiana, New Mexico and Mississippi, along with smaller outlets.

That does not mean every carton sold in those states is included. Distribution geography is a first screen; the side code and date are the decisive check.

The FDA-posted table lists Kroger cartons containing 12, 18, 30 and 60 eggs across large, extra-large, medium and jumbo grades. It also lists Simple Truth cage-free brown eggs in 12-, 18- and 24-count packages.

Brookshire’s entries range from six eggs to 60. Country Morning entries include 12-count, 18-count and 2½-dozen packages. The table also includes a Sunups 2½-dozen package and several 15- or 30-dozen bulk foodservice cases.

The published list contains 33 product rows. Some use UPCs; bulk foodservice cases are marked without a UPC. Every row uses the Julian range 157 to 184 and the July 20–Aug. 17 date window.

The company says it identified the issue through environmental monitoring and a root-cause analysis at its two Texas farms. It says it is not distributing fresh eggs produced at those farms while the recall is active.

The announcement says Midwest Poultry Services was not aware of any specific illnesses linked to its products when the notice was published July 22. That is a company statement posted by FDA, not proof that no later reports will emerge.

FDA explicitly labels the page a company announcement and says posting it does not constitute agency endorsement. The recall reason on the federal page is the potential for Salmonella Enteritidis contamination.

The notice urges consumers not to eat affected products and to return them to the original place of purchase for a refund. The essential comparison is three-part: plant code, Julian date and sell-by or best-by date.

A brand match without those code and date matches is not enough to identify an affected carton. Conversely, a matching code and date should not be dismissed because the package size or store looks unfamiliar; the recall includes foodservice bulk cases as well as household cartons.

The recall quantity converts to 19,074,924 eggs if expressed as individual units. That arithmetic communicates scale, but the company reported the official quantity in dozens, and the carton codes—not the converted total—are what shoppers can use.

The Trump administration imposed new Section 301 tariffs on imports from 60 economies beginning July 24, using foreign governments’ treatment of forced-labor goods as the stated basis for duties generally set at 10% or 12.5%.

The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative announced final action July 23 after investigations that began in March. USTR says the process included two rounds of public hearings, more than 2,100 public comments and consultations with more than 45 governments.

The additional duties apply to covered products entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, at or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern time on July 24. The implementation notice includes a limited transit exception for goods already loaded and in final transit before that time if they enter by July 28.

Seventeen economies receive the 10% rate: Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Canada, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, Mexico, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago and the United Kingdom.

USTR says those economies either have a forced-labor import prohibition, committed to adopt and enforce one through a reciprocal trade agreement or operate a partial regime that blocks some forced-labor goods.

Products from the European Union and Taiwan receive a special calculation intended to bring the combined most-favored-nation and Section 301 rate to 10% when the ordinary tariff is below 10%. Products already carrying an MFN rate of at least 10% receive no additional Section 301 duty under that calculation.

Japan, South Korea and Switzerland receive a similar calculation using a 12.5% threshold. Other investigated economies generally face a 12.5% additional duty.

The action is broad, but it is not universal. USTR exempted informational materials, donations, accompanied baggage, articles already subject to Section 232 tariffs and specified products that the agency says present supply, disruption or effectiveness concerns. The legally controlling product lists appear in the notice’s annexes.

The administration describes the policy as pressure on trading partners that have not imposed and effectively enforced bans on imports made with forced labor.

That description does not mean every product imported from a covered economy has been found to involve forced labor. The duties apply by economy and tariff classification based on USTR’s findings about government policy and enforcement.

The action also creates a bargaining mechanism. A trading partner can receive more favorable treatment if it adopts or commits to enforce an import prohibition. USTR says Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka and Trinidad and Tobago adopted prohibitions after the investigations began, while Jordan made a commitment through a reciprocal trade agreement.

The tariffs are collected from importers at the U.S. border. Foreign governments do not directly pay them. Importers may absorb the cost, pass it to customers, renegotiate contracts, shift suppliers or stop importing affected products.

The economic effect will depend heavily on the annexes. A headline rate says little about a particular product until its tariff classification, ordinary duty and exemption status are known.

The final notice also contemplates tariff-rate quotas for certain textile and apparel trade involving Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia and Malaysia. Those provisions are intended to encourage the use of U.S. cotton and textile inputs.

Legal and diplomatic disputes are likely to focus on whether USTR’s findings adequately support broad economy-wide duties, whether the remedy fits the identified practices and how the agency changes rates when a government reforms its import system.

For businesses and consumers, the immediate practical question is narrower: which products entered after July 24 now carry an additional duty, and who ultimately bears that cost?

articles.body:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order July 24 directing federal agencies to identify ways to pressure the Smithsonian Institution and ordering temporary signs on federal property used to approach the National Museum of American History.

Executive Order 14415 adopts the conclusions of a White House review that accuses Smithsonian leadership of presenting American history through an ideological framework. Those conclusions are the administration’s claims, not findings from an independent court or adjudicative body.

The order directs the Interior Department, Office of Management and Budget, General Services Administration and White House Domestic Policy Council to identify and use available legal authorities to advance the administration’s policy.

The listed mechanisms include statutes, regulations, executive actions, funding conditions and contract conditions.

The order separately directs the National Park Service to place temporary signs on NPS-maintained sidewalks, walkways and land used by visitors approaching the National Museum of American History.

The signs are supposed to tell visitors about the White House report, state that museum exhibits should be renovated and direct visitors to sources the administration considers accurate.

The order also calls for temporary signs or exhibits on Park Service property addressing the museum’s treatment of the 56 signers of the Declaration of Independence during the country’s 250th-anniversary year.

The Smithsonian is not an ordinary executive-branch department. Congress established it as an independent federal trust instrumentality. Its governing authority belongs to a 17-member Board of Regents that includes the chief justice, vice president, members of Congress and private citizens.

The board appoints the Smithsonian secretary and establishes major institutional policies. The president does not ordinarily supervise museum content in the same way the president directs a cabinet department.

The executive order therefore does not simply command the Smithsonian secretary to rewrite an exhibit. Instead, it tells executive agencies to use authorities they already possess and uses a more direct route where executive control is clearer: National Park Service property outside the museum.

That approach can produce disputes over appropriations, contracts, federal property and coercion. An agency may possess authority over a grant or contract without possessing authority to dictate scholarship. Whether a particular condition is lawful will depend on the statute, appropriation and agreement involved.

The Smithsonian’s Board of Regents has described the institution as nonpartisan and defended the secretary’s governing role. The board has also said it expects unbiased content and has directed leadership to report on changes.

The disagreement is therefore larger than a fight over one label. It concerns which institution defines historical neutrality, how executive agencies can use money and property to influence an independent federal institution and whether the administration can place its own interpretive message outside a museum it does not directly govern.

The order says implementation must comply with applicable law and remain subject to available appropriations. Those clauses leave agencies to determine which actions they believe are legally available.

The next meaningful developments will be the wording and placement of the signs, agency implementation plans, the Board of Regents’ response and any congressional or legal challenge.

articles.body:
Nearly two-thirds of the sustainable-development targets the United Nations can measure are moving too slowly or have slipped below their 2015 baselines, leaving the 2030 agenda with less than five years to turn broad gains into faster progress.

The Sustainable Development Goals Report 2026 evaluates 139 targets with sufficient trend data. It classifies 36% as on track or making moderate progress, 49% as moving too slowly and 15% as below their 2015 baselines.

Those shares add to 100% because they sort the measurable targets into three progress bands. They are not the percentage of countries succeeding, and they do not mean 64% of individual people are worse off.

The report says nearly 1 billion people gained access to safely managed drinking water since 2015, while 1.2 billion gained safely managed sanitation. Global electricity access reached 92% in 2024.

Digital access expanded even faster: the UN puts internet use at 74% in 2025, up from 40% in 2015. Those are consequential changes across a decade, and they explain why the report describes the goals as producing results at scale rather than as a uniform failure.

The same report estimates that 2.3 billion people experienced moderate or severe food insecurity in 2024. It says 273 million children and young people remained out of school even after 110 million more entered education since 2015.

Those figures measure different problems with different methods and reference years. They should not be combined into one population total because people can appear in more than one indicator and the underlying datasets are not synchronized.

The report says official development assistance fell 23.1% in 2025, the largest annual drop on its measure. It also places the annual financing gap for the goals at roughly $4 trillion.

A financing gap is an estimate of the difference between projected needs and available resources, not an invoice that one institution can settle. Its value is diagnostic: the UN is arguing that progress cannot accelerate at the required rate while concessional finance retreats and debt burdens rise.

Adding the 49% moving too slowly to the 15% below baseline yields 64% of assessable targets outside the report’s on-track-or-moderate category. That is the clearest summary of pace, but it applies only to the 139 targets for which the UN says reliable historical trends can be computed.

Targets without sufficient trend data are not silently counted as failures. The report is explicit about its assessment base, and changes in data availability or methodology can alter future comparisons as well as real-world progress.

The time horizon is equally important. The goals were adopted in 2015 for achievement by 2030, so an indicator can improve substantially and still be classified as too slow if its observed trajectory does not reach the target. Progress and adequate pace are separate judgments in the UN framework.

The result is neither a victory lap nor a declaration that the agenda is beyond recovery. It is a split-screen: demonstrable gains in water, sanitation, electricity and internet access, paired with a majority of measurable targets still moving too slowly or backward.

What the 64% headline can—and cannot—say

Adding the 49% moving too slowly to the 15% below baseline yields 64% of assessable targets outside the report’s on-track-or-moderate category. That is the clearest summary of pace, but it applies only to the 139 targets for which the UN says reliable historical trends can be computed.

Targets without sufficient trend data are not silently counted as failures. The report is explicit about its assessment base, and changes in data availability or methodology can alter future comparisons as well as real-world progress.

The time horizon is equally important. The goals were adopted in 2015 for achievement by 2030, so an indicator can improve substantially and still be classified as too slow if its observed trajectory does not reach the target. Progress and adequate pace are separate judgments in the UN framework.

The result is neither a victory lap nor a declaration that the agenda is beyond recovery. It is a split-screen: demonstrable gains in water, sanitation, electricity and internet access, paired with a majority of measurable targets still moving too slowly or backward.

The report and its official Statistics Division hub supply the 139-target assessment, progress shares, access gains, food-security and education estimates, assistance decline and financing-gap estimate.

articles.body:
U.S. construction spending barely moved in June, but the flat headline concealed a much weaker picture than a year earlier and sharply different paths across building sectors.

The Census Bureau estimated work put in place at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $2.1665 trillion, down 0.1% from a revised May rate of $2.1685 trillion. The agency’s sampling range around that monthly change includes zero, meaning the data do not establish that underlying spending actually fell rather than held steady.

Compared with June 2025, the estimate was 3.2% lower. During the first half of 2026, the value of construction put in place totaled an estimated $1.0469 trillion, 3.5% below the same six months a year earlier.

Private construction ran at a $1.6225 trillion annual pace, down 0.1% from May. Public construction was estimated at $544.1 billion and described by Census as virtually unchanged from the prior month.

Those figures are annualized rates: they describe what spending would look like over a year if June’s seasonally adjusted pace continued. They are not the dollars actually paid during the month. Census also reports the values in current dollars, so changes can reflect both the amount of work and changes in prices.

Residential construction was estimated at an $889.4 billion annual rate, 0.3% below May and 4.7% below June 2025. Private residential work—by far the larger piece—was down 4.7% from a year earlier.

The broad nonresidential estimate was only 2.1% below a year earlier, but its components were far from uniform. Manufacturing construction was estimated at $172.7 billion, down 21.4% from June 2025. Private manufacturing accounted for almost all of that category and was down 22.0%.

Office construction moved the other way. The annualized estimate reached $132.8 billion, 12.5% above June 2025. Private office work was up 15.1%, while public office construction was lower than a year earlier.

Conservation and development recorded the largest percentage increase among the listed broad categories, up 31.8% from a year earlier to a $16.6 billion annual rate. It is a much smaller category than highways, power or manufacturing, so a large percentage change has a limited effect on the national total.

Public highway and street construction, the largest public category, was estimated at $150.9 billion. That was 0.1% below May but 3.1% above June 2025. Public transportation construction was 3.8% higher than a year earlier.

The Census Bureau cautions that monthly estimates can be irregular. It says two months may be needed to establish an underlying trend for total construction and as many as eight months for individual categories.

June is also preliminary. The average absolute change between the preliminary estimate and first revision is 0.65% for total construction, 0.75% for private construction and 0.59% for public construction—larger than the reported one-month movement in the headline total.

The durable signal in this release is therefore not a statistically clear 0.1% monthly drop. It is the broader year-over-year decline and the widening gap between categories: manufacturing building substantially lower, office work higher and public infrastructure mostly stable to modestly above last year.

U.S. commercial crude oil inventories fell by 7.2 million barrels during the week ending July 24 as refineries increased their processing rate, according to the Energy Information Administration’s latest Weekly Petroleum Status Report.

Commercial crude stocks, excluding the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, stood at 404.5 million barrels. EIA said that level was about 6% below the five-year average for this time of year. Crude held in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve declined by 3.8 million barrels to 307.7 million.

Refinery inputs averaged 17.3 million barrels per day, an increase of 271,000 barrels per day from the previous week. Refineries operated at 97.2% of operable capacity, while gasoline production averaged 9.9 million barrels per day and distillate production averaged 5.4 million.

Crude oil imports averaged 5.7 million barrels per day, down 124,000 barrels per day from the previous week. Over the latest four-week period, imports averaged about 5.7 million barrels per day, 7% below the comparable period a year earlier.

Motor gasoline inventories were nearly unchanged at 211.3 million barrels and remained about 7% below their five-year seasonal average. Distillate inventories increased by 1.1 million barrels to 110.6 million but were still about 10% below the five-year average.

Propane and propylene inventories increased by 2.5 million barrels to 102.3 million. EIA said those stocks were 34% above the five-year average for this time of year. Total commercial petroleum inventories declined by 3.7 million barrels during the week.

EIA’s products-supplied measure, which the agency describes as an approximation of petroleum demand, averaged 20.3 million barrels per day over four weeks. That was 2.3% below the same period a year earlier. Gasoline supplied was down 0.3%, while distillate supplied was up 4.7% and jet fuel supplied was up 5.8%.

Energy prices remained sharply above year-earlier levels. West Texas Intermediate crude was $91.74 per barrel on July 24, up $8.31 from the previous week and $25.36 from a year earlier. The national average retail price for regular gasoline reached $4.096 per gallon on July 27, while diesel averaged $5.313 per gallon.

The weekly figures are preliminary estimates based primarily on company submissions for the period ending at 7 a.m. on Friday. EIA may revise weekly data as more complete information becomes available, and independent rounding can cause components not to sum exactly to totals.

articles.body:
The U.S. economy grew at a 1.5 percent annual rate in the second quarter of 2026, slowing from a 2.1 percent pace in the first quarter, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis’s advance estimate released Thursday.

The headline slowdown masked a sharper rebound in household demand. Real personal consumption expenditures increased at a 3.2 percent annual rate after rising 0.5 percent in the first quarter. Spending on goods rose 5.2 percent, while spending on services increased 2.2 percent.

Fixed investment also remained strong, increasing 7.0 percent. Equipment investment rose 15.2 percent and investment in intellectual property products increased 8.8 percent. Nonresidential structures fell 5.0 percent, while residential investment increased 1.5 percent after declining in the first quarter.

Government consumption expenditures and gross investment fell 0.8 percent after rising 4.4 percent in the first quarter. Federal spending declined 4.1 percent, driven by a 12.9 percent drop in nondefense spending, while state and local spending increased 1.1 percent.

BEA said the decline in federal nondefense spending primarily reflected sales of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. In the national accounts, those sales reduce government consumption expenditures, but the oil is reflected elsewhere in GDP, so the transactions do not directly reduce total GDP.

Exports increased 4.5 percent, while imports rose 11.5 percent. Imports are subtracted in the calculation of GDP, so faster import growth weighed on the headline rate even as it reflected continued U.S. demand for foreign goods.

Price growth accelerated during the quarter. The price index for gross domestic purchases increased 5.7 percent, compared with 3.6 percent in the first quarter. The personal consumption expenditures price index increased 5.1 percent, while the index excluding food and energy rose 3.4 percent.

One measure of underlying private demand looked stronger than the headline GDP figure. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers, which combines consumer spending and private fixed investment, increased 3.9 percent after rising 1.7 percent in the first quarter.

The figures are an advance estimate, not a final count. Quarterly growth rates are seasonally adjusted and expressed at annual rates, meaning the 1.5 percent figure describes the quarter’s pace if it continued for a full year. BEA is scheduled to publish its second estimate, along with an initial estimate of corporate profits, on August 26.

The report therefore shows slower overall output growth alongside firmer private domestic demand and faster prices. It does not, by itself, establish whether the economy is entering or avoiding a recession; that judgment requires a broader set of employment, income, production and sales data.

articles.body:
The U.S. economy grew at a 1.5% annual rate in the second quarter of 2026, slowing from 2.1% in the first quarter, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis' advance estimate released Thursday.

The headline rate is seasonally adjusted and annualized, meaning it describes how much the economy would grow over a full year if the quarter's pace continued. The underlying quarter-to-quarter increase was 0.4%. Because this is an advance estimate built partly from incomplete source data, it can be revised when BEA publishes its second estimate on August 26.

Consumer spending accelerated sharply despite the slower headline result. Real personal consumption expenditures increased at a 3.2% annual rate after rising 0.5% in the first quarter. Spending on goods rose 5.2%, while services spending increased 2.2%.

A measure designed to track domestic private demand was considerably stronger than GDP. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers, which combines consumer spending with private fixed investment, increased 3.9% after rising 1.7% in the first quarter. That measure excludes inventories, exports, imports and government spending, components that can make the headline GDP figure more volatile.

Business investment remained a source of growth. Real fixed investment increased 7.0%, including an 8.4% increase in nonresidential investment. Equipment investment rose 15.2%, and investment in intellectual property products increased 8.8%. Residential investment turned positive, rising 1.5% after falling 7.8% in the first quarter.

Trade restrained the headline rate because imports grew faster than exports. Real exports increased 4.5%, while imports increased 11.5%. Imports are subtracted in the GDP calculation because GDP measures domestic production, not because imports are inherently a loss to the economy.

Government spending declined at a 0.8% annual rate after increasing 4.4% in the first quarter. Federal spending fell 4.1%, while state and local spending increased 1.1%. BEA said the federal decline was led by nondefense consumption expenditures and partly reflected crude-oil sales from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which are treated as a reduction in government consumption.

Price measures accelerated during the quarter. The price index for gross domestic purchases increased 5.7%, compared with 3.6% in the first quarter. The quarterly PCE price index increased 5.1%, while the index excluding food and energy increased 3.4%. These are annualized quarter-to-quarter rates and should not be confused with the separate year-over-year inflation figures.

BEA's accompanying June report showed personal income rising 0.2%, current-dollar consumer spending rising 0.3% and inflation-adjusted spending rising 0.4% for the month. The personal saving rate was 2.7%. The monthly PCE price index declined 0.1% from May but remained 3.7% above its level a year earlier.

The report therefore shows slower overall growth alongside stronger household spending and private domestic demand. It does not by itself establish that the economy is entering a recession or that inflation has permanently changed direction. The advance GDP estimate, June income figures and historical data are all subject to revision, including during BEA's annual update scheduled for September 30.

articles.body:
Two unusually low-flying research aircraft are set to trace a tight grid over eastern Kansas, gathering magnetic and radiometric measurements for a new map of the rocks beneath the region.

The U.S. Geological Survey said flights could begin as soon as late July. The fixed-wing planes will follow preplanned lines about 980 feet, or 300 meters, apart while maintaining a nominal terrain clearance of about 260 feet, or 80 meters.

An Air Tractor AT-504 and a Pilatus PC-6 will carry sensors in an elongated boom, or “stinger,” extending from the main cabin. USGS said the instruments are passive, emit nothing that poses a risk to people, animals or plants, and will not collect photography or video.

The contractor, New Resolution Geophysics Exploration USA, will fly during daylight. Pilots are specially trained and approved for low-level work and coordinate with the Federal Aviation Administration, according to the agency.

Operations will be based at Coffey County, Salina Regional and Newton City-County airports. The announced route covers a broad band of counties from the Kansas City region south toward the Oklahoma line and west toward Salina and Wichita.

The survey centers on the Nemaha Uplift, a buried ridge extending from southern Nebraska into central Oklahoma. The region includes coal and petroleum resources, rocks with critical-mineral potential and the Humboldt Fault Zone, an active fault system that parallels the uplift.

USGS and the Kansas Geological Survey say the measurements can sharpen geologic maps used to assess mineral resources, geologic hydrogen, groundwater, earthquake hazards, infrastructure conditions and land-use questions. The flight data alone will not establish that an economically recoverable deposit exists.

The work is part of the federal Earth Mapping Resources Initiative, which combines airborne geophysics with geochemistry, lidar, hyperspectral surveys and field mapping. USGS says the resulting datasets will be released publicly through ScienceBase.

Because the planes will fly much lower and in straighter, more repetitive patterns than typical traffic, they may be conspicuous from the ground. The agency says the schedule depends on weather, aircraft availability and other operational conditions.

The mapped boundary is provisional. USGS listed additional counties in Kansas, Missouri, Oklahoma and Arkansas that could be added, so the final footprint may be wider than the initial blue outline.

articles.body:
Congress held two Iran war-powers votes on July 23. The House passed a concurrent resolution 214-208. The Senate rejected a motion to discharge a separate joint resolution 47-49.

Neither event, standing alone, ordered the military to stop fighting.

Understanding why requires separating the Constitution, the 1973 War Powers Resolution and the different forms of congressional action.

The Constitution gives Congress powers to declare war, fund the armed forces and make rules governing them. It names the president commander in chief. Presidents and Congress have disputed the boundary between those powers throughout the country’s history.

Congress enacted the War Powers Resolution over President Richard Nixon’s veto in 1973. The statute was designed to require consultation and reporting and to create procedures for ending military action that lacks congressional authorization.

The law generally requires the president to report specified deployments within 48 hours. Section 5(b) then provides a 60-day termination framework, with a possible 30-day period for safe removal, unless Congress declares war, enacts a specific authorization, extends the deadline or is unable to meet because of an attack on the United States.

The House used Section 5(c), which says forces engaged in unauthorized hostilities shall be removed if Congress directs removal by concurrent resolution.

A concurrent resolution must pass both chambers but is not presented to the president. The Senate did not approve the House resolution Thursday.

The Senate vote concerned a different device. S.J. Res. 180 is a joint resolution. If both chambers passed it, it would go to the president. The president could sign it or veto it, and Congress could override a veto only with two-thirds support in both chambers.

The Senate did not reach final passage. It rejected a motion to discharge the joint resolution from committee, preventing that procedural route from moving the measure forward.

The concurrent-resolution mechanism in Section 5(c) also carries a constitutional complication. In 1983, the Supreme Court held in INS v. Chadha that Congress generally could not exercise legislative power through a resolution that bypassed the Constitution’s bicameralism and presentment requirements. Chadha did not decide a War Powers Resolution case, but it cast doubt on the enforceability of Section 5(c)’s original design.

Congress later created expedited procedures for joint resolutions and bills directing removal of forces. Those procedures preserve presidential presentment and the possibility of a veto.

The House vote nevertheless has practical significance. It shows that a majority of the chamber does not accept the hostilities as congressionally authorized. It can shape oversight, appropriations negotiations and the political cost of continuing operations.

The failed Senate motion also matters. It shows that opponents did not have enough votes to force the separate joint resolution out of committee through that procedure.

Congress retains stronger tools than a one-chamber vote. It can prohibit the use of appropriated funds for specified operations, enact a binding joint resolution, pass a limited authorization for use of military force, impose reporting conditions or refuse future funding.

Each option requires more agreement than the House demonstrated Thursday. A funding restriction or veto-proof measure would require durable majorities in both chambers.

The most accurate description of the current position is therefore narrow: the House approved a removal directive, the Senate blocked a procedural path for a separate joint resolution, and military operations did not automatically end.

articles.body:
Section 301 is one of the federal government’s main tools for responding to foreign trade practices that the United States considers unfair.

It is not a single tariff. It is an investigative and enforcement framework established by the Trade Act of 1974.

The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative can initiate an investigation into a foreign government’s act, policy or practice. USTR then determines whether the conduct violates a trade agreement or is unjustifiable, unreasonable or discriminatory and burdens or restricts U.S. commerce.

If the statutory conditions are met, the trade representative can take responsive action. Tariffs are one option. Other responses can include restrictions on services, suspension of trade-agreement benefits or negotiation of an agreement intended to eliminate the disputed practice.

The process matters because it produces an administrative record. USTR identifies the practice, publishes notices, accepts comments, consults affected governments, conducts hearings where required, issues findings and publishes the final action.

That record does not make the decision politically neutral or legally unassailable. The executive branch still defines the challenged practice, evaluates the evidence, connects it to U.S. commerce and selects the remedy.

The new forced-labor action illustrates the law’s breadth. USTR investigated 60 economies for failing to impose and effectively enforce restrictions on imports produced with forced labor. It concluded that the failures were unreasonable and burdened or restricted U.S. commerce.

USTR then imposed duties generally set at 10% or 12.5%, with exemptions and special calculations for several trading partners.

The United States has long prohibited imports produced wholly or partly with forced labor. USTR’s theory is that weak foreign import controls allow forced-labor goods to circulate through global markets, distort competition and undermine firms that avoid such production.

The remedy is not limited to a shipment shown to contain forced-labor inputs. It applies broadly to covered imports from an economy based on the agency’s findings about that government’s laws and enforcement.

That design raises several questions.

How closely must the remedy fit the challenged practice? A broad tariff affects lawful goods as well as suspect supply chains.

How will USTR decide that a government has improved enough to qualify for lower rates or removal?

What evidence distinguishes effective enforcement from a prohibition that exists only on paper?

How do the new duties interact with ordinary tariffs, Section 232 measures, trade agreements and product exemptions?

Section 301 has supported major trade actions for decades, including extensive tariffs on Chinese goods. Its flexibility makes it powerful. The same flexibility makes the quality of the investigation and the precision of the final notice especially important.

Readers evaluating any Section 301 action should look for five things: the foreign practice USTR identifies; the evidence supporting the finding; the statutory category invoked; the remedy selected; and the process for modification or termination.

The tariff is charged to importers when covered goods enter the United States. It is not a bill sent to a foreign treasury. Who ultimately pays depends on contracts, market power, supply alternatives and pricing decisions throughout the distribution chain.

Section 301 gives the administration leverage. It does not eliminate the need to ask whether the leverage is lawful, proportionate and likely to produce the stated result.

articles.body:
The Smithsonian Institution is federal, public, private and independent at the same time.

That unusual structure is central to understanding the Trump administration’s effort to influence the National Museum of American History.

Congress created the Smithsonian in 1846 to administer the bequest of British scientist James Smithson for the increase and diffusion of knowledge. The institution describes itself as an independent federal trust instrumentality and a public-private partnership.

It is not a cabinet department and is not organized as a typical executive agency.

Its governing authority belongs to a 17-member Board of Regents.

The chief justice of the United States and the vice president serve as ex officio Regents. Six members come from Congress: three senators and three representatives. Nine citizen Regents are appointed through joint resolutions of Congress signed by the president after nomination through the board’s process.

The board appoints the Smithsonian secretary, establishes major policies, oversees strategy and budgets and evaluates leadership.

No single branch therefore controls the institution cleanly.

Congress created the Smithsonian, provides substantial appropriations and participates directly in governance.

The president signs the joint resolutions appointing citizen Regents, and the vice president sits on the board, but the president does not ordinarily appoint the Smithsonian secretary or manage museum exhibits as the head of a cabinet agency would.

The chief justice serves as chancellor, bringing the head of the judicial branch into the same governing arrangement.

Private money matters too. The Smithsonian receives gifts, grants, research contracts and earned revenue in addition to federal appropriations.

This hybrid design was intended to support a national public mission while preserving institutional independence. It also creates multiple leverage points.

Congress can legislate, investigate and use appropriations.

The Board of Regents governs the Smithsonian and appoints its secretary.

Executive agencies can affect contracts, implementation and surrounding federal property where they possess statutory authority.

Private donors and partners can influence which projects are financially possible, though they do not possess formal governing power.

Trump’s July 24 order reflects those limits. Rather than directly ordering the secretary to rewrite exhibits, it tells executive agencies to examine laws, regulations, contracts and funding. It also directs the National Park Service to place signs on NPS-maintained approaches to the museum.

That could produce competing messages side by side: Smithsonian exhibits under the institution’s authority and administration-approved warnings on adjacent federal property.

The order may also provoke disputes over whether agencies are applying funding or contract conditions lawfully and whether they are attempting to coerce an institution Congress designed to have independent governance.

The Smithsonian’s Board of Regents has defended the secretary’s authority and described the institution as nonpartisan. At the same time, it has directed leadership to set expectations for unbiased content and report on changes.

Both the administration and the board therefore claim to be protecting accuracy and nonpartisanship. They disagree about the substance of those terms and who has authority to enforce them.

The practical answer to who controls the Smithsonian is: several institutions do, in different ways.

The Regents govern it. Congress created and funds it. Executive agencies control some money, contracts and property. Courts can resolve legal disputes when a suitable case reaches them. Private supporters exert financial influence without final legal authority.

That divided structure is why the current confrontation will unfold through implementation, appropriations, governance and possibly litigation rather than through one presidential command.

articles.body:
Nearly two-thirds of Americans born from 1980 through 1984 received at least one form of work-related training outside regular degree-granting schooling between ages 18 and 38, according to a Bureau of Labor Statistics summary published July 27.

The National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1997 found that 65.4% of the cohort received some form of training during that period. Formal employer training was the most common listed category at 29.1%, followed by vocational, technical or trade training at 26.5%.

Other reported categories included school-based training at 14.1%, training at work provided by an outside organization at 11.7%, training outside work at 11.1%, government training at 7.5% and apprenticeships at 3.6%. BLS also placed 14.3% in an “other” training category.

Participation differed substantially by educational attainment. BLS reported that 44% of people who had not completed high school received some type of training by their 39th birthday, compared with 61% of high school graduates who had not attended college, 71% of people with some college or an associate degree and 66% of people with a bachelor’s degree or higher.

The type of training also varied with education. Employer training reached 35.7% among people with a bachelor’s degree or higher, compared with 10.5% among people who had not completed high school. Vocational, technical or trade training was more common among high school graduates with no college and people with some college or an associate degree, at 32.3% and 32.5%, respectively.

BLS defines the training measure as instruction outside regular schooling that offers an academic diploma or degree. The category can include vocational and trade programs, apprenticeships, employer programs, government programs and other instruction intended to improve job skills, prepare someone for a new job or make it easier to find work.

The results come from a longitudinal survey that follows the same people over time rather than drawing a new sample each year. About 9,000 participants, born from 1980 through 1984, were first interviewed in 1997 when they were ages 12 to 17. They were interviewed for the 21st time in 2023 and 2024, when they were ages 38 to 44.

That design lets researchers measure whether a person received training at any point across roughly two decades. It does not describe the share of all workers receiving training in a single year, and it does not by itself establish that training caused later changes in wages, employment or job stability.

The survey represents people in this birth cohort who were living in the United States when the study began in 1997. BLS says it does not represent immigrants born from 1980 through 1984 who moved to the United States after 1997.

BLS reissued the underlying news release on July 17 to correct date and age ranges in one table and remove an extra digit from another table’s title. The agency said those corrections did not change any data estimates.

The findings show that training outside degree programs was common but unevenly distributed. Employer-provided training rose sharply with educational attainment, while vocational and trade training was most prevalent among people with a high school education or some college.

The data are cumulative through age 38 and specific to one generation. They provide a long-run view of how often early-1980s-born Americans encountered job training, not a real-time measure of the current labor market or the availability and quality of training programs today.

The World Bank Group's Board of Executive Directors has discussed a new six-year partnership framework for China that would place greater emphasis on knowledge sharing, selective financing and lessons intended to apply beyond the country itself.

The Country Partnership Framework covers fiscal years 2026 through 2031. The World Bank described it as a new phase in a relationship that began in 1980 and has gradually shifted as China's economy and development needs changed.

The framework identifies three priority areas: enabling productivity-led growth and better jobs; strengthening human capital and social protection as the population ages; and expanding resilient, sustainable infrastructure while protecting and restoring natural ecosystems.

Those themes track priorities in China's 15th Five-Year Plan, including stronger domestic demand, job creation, updated social protection and the country's stated goals of peaking carbon emissions before 2030 and reaching carbon neutrality by 2060.

The World Bank said lending from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development is phasing down. The relationship is expected to rely more heavily on policy knowledge, innovation, mutual learning and targeted financing rather than broad development lending.

One part of that shift is the sharing of China's experience in areas such as ecosystem restoration, water management and agricultural productivity when other World Bank Group countries request it. The bank said those efforts would be linked to its Knowledge Bank and the China-WBG Global Center for Ecological Systems and Transitions.

The board discussion establishes the framework for cooperation, but it does not by itself set the value or terms of every future project. Individual operations and financing decisions would still require their own review and approval processes.

The World Bank said China is increasingly both a user and provider of development knowledge, as well as a contributor and donor to the institution. That evolving role is central to the framework's focus on ideas and practices that could be useful in other emerging markets.

The practical effect of the framework will become clearer as specific projects, advisory work and knowledge-sharing programs are announced during the 2026–31 period.

The World Bank has approved $375.9 million for equipment intended to stabilize Pakistan’s transmission grid and move wind power that existing bottlenecks keep from reaching customers.

The financing, approved July 9, covers the first phase of a 10-year program called Boosting Energy Security through Transmission in Pakistan, or BEST-PAK. Its immediate engineering focus is voltage control at high-capacity substations rather than construction of a new wind farm.

World Bank estimates say the upgrades can unlock 640 megawatts of wind generation now being curtailed and enable the full use of 1,840 megawatts of wind capacity in southern Pakistan. Those are project objectives, not power already delivered by newly installed equipment.

Plans call for static synchronous compensators, known as STATCOMs, at three major 500-kilovolt substations. These power-electronics systems inject or absorb reactive power quickly, helping operators keep grid voltage within limits when supply and demand change.

Fixed reactors and capacitor banks are planned across 26 additional substations. Reactors can absorb reactive power when voltage is too high; capacitor banks can supply it when voltage is too low. Together, the devices address stability limits that can force operators to reduce generation even when turbines are available.

The project is also designed to make room for about 491 megawatts of planned private-sector renewable projects. Whether all of that capacity is built and connected depends on decisions beyond this World Bank financing.

Pakistan has committed to a 60% renewable share in its electricity mix by 2030 under its climate plan. The grid project can support that goal, but it does not by itself guarantee the target, determine future demand or resolve every financial problem in the power sector.

The physical specifications respond to two hazards that can disable substations: flooding and heat. New installations are to use elevated platforms where flood exposure demands it, and equipment must be rated to operate at temperatures up to 55 degrees Celsius, or 131 degrees Fahrenheit.

Those standards matter because transmission equipment loses performance and ages faster when temperatures exceed its design envelope. Elevation can protect critical gear from inundation, but it cannot eliminate every flood risk to access roads, communications or connected lines.

The World Bank estimates the project could avoid about 832,500 metric tons of carbon dioxide a year, or more than 20.8 million tons over 25 years. That is a modeled impact. It depends on the upgrades being completed, wind power displacing more carbon-intensive generation and the grid operating as assumed.

BEST-PAK is framed as more than an equipment purchase. The first phase also supports Pakistan’s plan to restructure the National Transmission & Dispatch Company into specialized successor organizations and strengthen governance and operating performance.

Institutional reform introduces its own execution risk. Dividing responsibilities can clarify accountability, but only if staffing, control-room authority, maintenance budgets, data and emergency procedures remain coordinated across the new entities.

The approval is therefore a financing milestone, not completion evidence. Procurement, installation, commissioning and measured reductions in curtailment will determine whether the project produces its advertised capacity and reliability gains.

The most useful public checks will be operational: which substations receive equipment, when each system enters service, how often wind is still curtailed and whether voltage and outage indicators improve. Until those data arrive, the World Bank figures are a detailed plan with explicit engineering targets.

More than 1,700 young athletes from more than 135 countries are due at Hayward Field this week for the World Athletics U20 Championships, a five-day meet that opens Wednesday with three distance finals, the men’s shot put and a mixed 4-by-400-meter relay.

The Aug. 5–9 championships are the 21st edition of the global under-20 meet and the second staged in Oregon. The last Oregon edition was held at the former Hayward Field in 2014; the rebuilt stadium later hosted the 2022 senior world championships.

World Athletics’ most recent event release gives the expected scale as more than 1,700 athletes from more than 135 countries. Those are organizer figures, not a final count of starters: accreditation, travel and late withdrawals can change the field before each event.

The first champion is scheduled to come from the men’s shot put at 7:50 p.m. local time Wednesday. The women’s and men’s 5,000-meter finals follow, and the mixed 4-by-400 closes the opening session at 8:50 p.m.

The women’s and men’s 100-meter finals anchor Thursday evening. Friday concentrates on qualifying and combined-events competition. World Athletics lists 12 finals for Saturday evening and 15 titles on Sunday, when the championships end with the women’s and men’s 4-by-400 relays.

One new feature is the mixed 4-by-100-meter relay. World Athletics’ published program places its first round Thursday morning and the final Saturday evening. The mixed 4-by-400 remains on the opening-night schedule.

The U20 championships sit at an unusual point in the sport. The competition awards world titles, but the field spans athletes whose bodies, coaching environments and experience are still changing quickly. A standout performance can signal elite potential without guaranteeing a senior career.

That makes restraint important in covering the meet. Boho News will report verified results and competition records without turning teenage athletes into permanent projections or publishing unnecessary personal details. Athlete eligibility and official result lists remain the governing sources.

The event’s medals use the same geometric tree-and-wings form as the Oregon 26 logo. Organizers describe the tree as a reference to the state’s landscape and the wings as a link to the winged-foot symbol of track and field and Oregon’s “She flies with her own wings” motto.

Ribbon colors distinguish the medals: blue for gold, red and orange for silver, and green for bronze. Podium athletes are also due to receive matching pins intended for a coach, family member, friend or teammate.

Published schedules are operational documents, not guarantees. Heat assignments, advancement, weather and competition appeals can alter the order or timing. The official World Athletics timetable and results system should be checked immediately before any event or result is reported.

The reliable opening-day frame is broader: a five-day global junior championship returns to Eugene, introduces a mixed sprint relay to the U20 program and begins awarding titles immediately. The results from Hayward Field—not pre-meet projections—will determine which athletes leave with the new Oregon-shaped medals.

The Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden will reopen its renovated outdoor space this fall with three new monumental heads by Yoshitomo Nara, beginning an annual series of artist commissions on the museum’s West Lawn.

“Yoshitomo Nara: Sentinels of Stillness” is scheduled to run from Oct. 31, 2026, through Nov. 7, 2027, the Smithsonian announced Tuesday. The presentation will bring “Long Tall Peace Sister,” “Smiling” and “Tiny Bright Round Eyes,” all dated 2025, to the National Mall.

Each work enlarges a palm-sized clay head Nara made in 2021. The finished sculptures are fabricated in aluminum and coated in white urethane paint, translating the irregularity of hand-shaped clay into forms intended for an outdoor public setting.

Hirshhorn Director Melissa Chiu said the show will establish a yearly West Lawn exhibition by a leading international artist. Anne Reeve, a Hirshhorn curator, organized the first installment, which the museum says will include free tours and art education.

The announcement describes the three heads as evoking childhood snowdrifts and as emphasizing how daylight changes across their surfaces. Those are the museum’s and artist’s interpretive frames; visitors will not be able to evaluate the installed works until the garden opens.

The new series is separate from the Hirshhorn’s permanent collection. The first show has a defined closing date in November 2027, and the museum says a different commissioned artist will follow on the lawn each year.

Nara’s sculpture practice predates the new works by decades. He began making figurative wood carvings in the mid-1980s, later worked with fiber-reinforced plastic, lacquer and urethane, and developed his ceramic practice during a 2007 residency in Shigaraki, Japan.

According to the Hirshhorn, Nara turned more deeply to hand-molded clay after the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and Fukushima nuclear disaster affected his home region. He conceived large-scale sculptural enlargements in 2020 and made the small heads behind the new trio the following year.

The museum’s account is biographical, not a claim that the new works document the disaster. The announced sculptures are presented as contemporary public art shaped by material process, memory and scale.

The sculpture garden closed for renovation in 2023. Its redesign by Hiroshi Sugimoto received approvals from the Commission of Fine Arts and the National Capital Planning Commission in 2022 after public consultation.

The Smithsonian says the reopening will add an expanded entrance from the National Mall and refresh the passage connecting the garden with the museum building and plaza. Those access changes matter because the original 1974 sunken design could be difficult to enter and navigate.

The museum has not attached a separate ticket price to the exhibition. The Hirshhorn’s public programs and galleries are free, although operating details can change before the Oct. 31 opening.

For now, the firm facts are the artists, titles, dates, materials and planned series. The appearance of the completed installation, its relationship to the redesigned lawn and the visitor experience remain future-facing until the site reopens.

bodyBlocks.text: The Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden will reopen its renovated outdoor space this fall with three new monumental heads by Yoshitomo Nara, beginning an annual series of artist commissions on the museum’s West Lawn.

“Yoshitomo Nara: Sentinels of Stillness” is scheduled to run from Oct. 31, 2026, through Nov. 7, 2027, the Smithsonian announced Tuesday. The presentation will bring “Long Tall Peace Sister,” “Smiling” and “Tiny Bright Round Eyes,” all dated 2025, to the National Mall.

Each work enlarges a palm-sized clay head Nara made in 2021. The finished sculptures are fabricated in aluminum and coated in white urethane paint, translating the irregularity of hand-shaped clay into forms intended for an outdoor public setting.
Three works begin a recurring commission

Hirshhorn Director Melissa Chiu said the show will establish a yearly West Lawn exhibition by a leading international artist. Anne Reeve, a Hirshhorn curator, organized the first installment, which the museum says will include free tours and art education.

The announcement describes the three heads as evoking childhood snowdrifts and as emphasizing how daylight changes across their surfaces. Those are the museum’s and artist’s interpretive frames; visitors will not be able to evaluate the installed works until the garden opens.

bodyBlocks.alt: Graphic lists the three 2025 sculptures announced for Yoshitomo Nara’s Hirshhorn West Lawn exhibition.
bodyBlocks.caption: The three announced works are enlargements of small clay heads Nara made in 2021. The graphic does not depict their appearance.
bodyBlocks.credit: Boho News graphic from Smithsonian records

bodyBlocks.text: The new series is separate from the Hirshhorn’s permanent collection. The first show has a defined closing date in November 2027, and the museum says a different commissioned artist will follow on the lawn each year.
The clay work grew from a turning point

Nara’s sculpture practice predates the new works by decades. He began making figurative wood carvings in the mid-1980s, later worked with fiber-reinforced plastic, lacquer and urethane, and developed his ceramic practice during a 2007 residency in Shigaraki, Japan.

According to the Hirshhorn, Nara turned more deeply to hand-molded clay after the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and Fukushima nuclear disaster affected his home region. He conceived large-scale sculptural enlargements in 2020 and made the small heads behind the new trio the following year.
